items.body_md:
On August 13, the debtor filed a motion to establish notice and procedures for the assumption and assignment of contracts and leases (Dkt. 86), the most consequential filing of this cycle given that a § 363 sale of the Pleasants Power Station is the stated exit path. An assumption-and-assignment procedures motion governs the mechanics by which the estate identifies executory contracts and unexpired leases it intends to transfer to a buyer — including cure-notice timelines, the process for counterparties to object to cure amounts or adequate assurance, and the deadline structure that will govern any sale closing. In a 1,278-MW coal-fired generation asset operating within PJM and carrying a counterparty roster that includes energy trading arrangements and PJM-related obligations, the universe of contracts subject to § 365 treatment is substantial, and the procedures order will set the objection and cure-dispute framework that counterparties and the estate must navigate before any § 363 sale closes. The content of Dkt. 86 is not fully reproduced in available record; the identity of any proposed stalking-horse bidder, cure-estimate methodology, or deadline structure will require a full-text pull and will be reported when confirmed.

Also filed August 13 were five additional employment and retention applications (Dkts. 81–85), beyond the Stretto administrative advisor application (Dkt. 79) and the interim compensation procedures motion (Dkt. 78) covered in yesterday's briefing. The identities of the five proposed professionals are not confirmed from available docket text and are unverified here; what confirmation looks like is the full-text pull of each application. As a cluster, they are substantive filings — each draws on estate resources and defines who bills the estate — but absent any indication of contest, they are routine at this stage of a Chapter 11. If any of the five engages a financial advisor, investment banker, or restructuring advisor with a sale mandate, that appointment would carry material weight for creditor recovery and will be elevated when confirmed. Dkts. 87–92, filed today, are pro hac vice motions and admissions for additional counsel — procedural and routine, requiring no further analysis.

The August 19 objection deadline for final approval of the prepetition tax order (Dkt. 49, authorizing up to $775,000 in prepetition tax and fee payments) remains the nearest hard date, now five days out, with no objection on the docket as of this briefing. The next concrete milestones are August 19 (tax-order objection deadline), September 2 (§ 341(a) meeting of creditors, 1:00 p.m. ET via Zoom), and September 3 (final hearings on wages, utility payments, and critical vendor orders). Dkt. 86's assumption-and-assignment procedures motion will require a hearing date; none is confirmed on the record, and the timing of that hearing relative to any § 363 sale motion will be the next structural question to watch.

items.lede: Today, Papaya Gaming's docket recorded Dkt. 68 — a Notice of Service — procedural and routine, carrying no bearing on recovery or timing.
items.body_md:
Today, Papaya Gaming's docket recorded Dkt. 68 — a Notice of Service — procedural and routine, carrying no bearing on recovery or timing.

With no substantive movement today, the active pressure point remains the two deposition notices filed August 11 (Dkts. 61–62), which signal that discovery is running in advance of the recognition hearing. 
Judge Walrath's temporary injunction — granted after she rejected Skillz's opposition — currently stays collection and enforcement against Papaya's U.S. assets, and that protection runs only until the recognition hearing resolves whether the Israeli proceeding qualifies for Chapter 15 recognition.
 The deposition activity suggests both sides are building evidentiary records for that hearing rather than treating the stay as settled ground. 
The Israeli court-supervised fund arrangement, under which Papaya is to hold approximately $100 million during 2026 with additional annual contributions, will be a central issue: its adequacy as a creditor-protection mechanism is the practical question the recognition hearing must answer.


For Skillz/Firy, the recognition hearing is the next inflection point — a denial would lift the stay and reopen collection on the $719 million disgorgement award and the approximately $10.1 million in attorneys' fees and costs. 
Judge Cote ordered approximately $719 million in disgorgement plus approximately $10.1 million in attorneys' fees and costs, and declined to impose a permanent injunction against Papaya's operations.
 No date for the recognition hearing has surfaced on the public docket record provided; that date, once set, is the next concrete milestone governing the stay's duration and creditor recovery timing.

items.body_md:
Today, Judge Vince Chhabria convened the further case management conference in *Kadrey v. Meta Platforms, Inc.*, No. 3:23-cv-03417 (N.D. Cal.), at 11:00 AM Pacific by Zoom videoconference, the time having been advanced by the clerk's notice filed yesterday (Dkt. 809). The operative framing document before Chhabria was the Joint Case Management Statement filed Wednesday by counsel for sixteen named plaintiffs including Richard Kadrey, Ta-Nehisi Coates, Sarah Silverman, and Jacqueline Woodson (Dkt. 808). No minute entry or text order from the conference has posted to the public docket as of this briefing; the minute entry, when it appears, is the controlling source for whatever scheduling or substantive direction Chhabria announced. The two live threads heading into the conference were the contributory infringement amendment posture and the downstream discovery schedule in the four related actions where Chhabria denied Meta's motion to quash on August 11 (Dkt. 807, covering Nos. 3:25-cv-09579, 3:26-cv-02333, 3:26-cv-03725, and 3:26-cv-04053); both were ripe for scheduling direction. The minute entry is the sole remaining milestone for today's proceedings and should be pulled as soon as it posts.

In *Getty Images (US), Inc. v. Stability AI, Inc. et al.*, No. 3:25-cv-06891 (N.D. Cal., Thompson, J.), Stability AI filed its opposition to Getty's administrative motion for leave to file a reply (Dkt. 71, August 12), completing the paper sequence on a disputed Local Rule 7-11 procedural point that opened with Getty's scheduling-variance motion on August 6 (Dkt. 68) and ran through Stability's opposition at Dkt. 69 (August 10) and Getty's leave motion at Dkt. 70 (August 11). The opposition was filed by Joseph Gratz on behalf of all three Stability AI entities. The substantive question underneath the dueling administrative motions is what scope of modification, if any, Judge Thompson grants to the existing case management and scheduling order — which sets private mediation completion by October 19, 2026, dispositive motions due March 12, 2027, and a jury trial window of January 18 through February 9, 2028. 
Judge Thompson denied most of Stability AI's motion to dismiss Getty's complaint in April 2026.
 
The only claim dismissed was Getty's DMCA CMI §1202(a) claim, for failure to allege intentional conduct, though Getty was granted leave to amend.
 That posture — nearly all claims surviving — gives the scheduling fight its stakes: any expansion of the briefing or discovery schedule directly affects how much ground Getty can develop before the dispositive-motion deadline. 
The UK High Court decided the parallel UK action on November 4, 2025, rejecting the "model weights as infringing copies" theory but finding limited trademark infringement on Getty watermarks reproduced in generated images; Getty was granted leave to appeal in December 2025.
 The appeal's outcome on the model-weights theory bears directly on the same theory Getty presses before Thompson. Judge Thompson's ruling on the leave-to-reply motion is the next concrete event in this action; responses on Dkt. 70 were due August 17, 2026, making a decision possible in the coming days.

In *Encyclopaedia Britannica, Inc. and Merriam-Webster, Inc. v. OpenAI, Inc. et al.*, No. 1:26-cv-02097 (S.D.N.Y., Stein, J.), the memo endorsement filed August 12 (Dkt. 59) is the only movement since the previous edition. As noted, the document text remains unavailable on the public record; the docket sequence — Dkts. 56 through 59 spanning August 5–12 — is consistent with the court working through interim case management obligations that arise within the existing stay tied to summary judgment proceedings in the broader OpenAI MDL (No. 1:25-md-03143). Nothing in the available record alters that stay posture. *Hachette v. Google (Gemini)*, No. 1:26-cv-05870 (S.D.N.Y., Preska, J.), and *Hachette v. Meta (Llama)*, No. 1:26-cv-03689 (S.D.N.Y., Castel, J.), recorded no movement; the Google transfer motion remains under submission before Preska, and the next milestone in the Meta action is the September 15, 2026 initial conference before Judge Castel at 3:00 PM in Courtroom 11D. *Thomson Reuters v. Ross Intelligence*, No. 25-2153 (3d Cir.), likewise recorded no movement, with the panel of Judges Restrepo, Montgomery-Reeves, and Bove continuing to deliberate following the June 11 oral argument.

items.lede: On August 12, at least two parties filed oppositions (Dkts. 51 and 52) and one filed an objection (Dkt. 56) against what the docket labels confirm are distinct contested matters, accompanied by a supporting declaration (Dkt. 53) and a stipulation (Dkt. 57) — the heaviest single day of adversarial activity in this case since the first-day hearing.
items.body_md:
On August 12, at least two parties filed oppositions (Dkts. 51 and 52) and one filed an objection (Dkt. 56) against what the docket labels confirm are distinct contested matters, accompanied by a supporting declaration (Dkt. 53) and a stipulation (Dkt. 57) — the heaviest single day of adversarial activity in this case since the first-day hearing. The docket does not yet identify the targets of those filings by description in the materials available to this desk, but the case context narrows the candidates sharply. The CRO compensation notice (Dkt. 43, filed August 5) carried an opposition deadline of August 19 and sought court authorization for insider-adjacent compensation — the CRO, Leslie Gladstone, being named in Dkt. 43's attachments — making it a live target for the U.S. Trustee or judgment creditors. The Manatt employment application (Dkt. 42, filed August 5) is the other obvious target; contested retention applications, particularly where the estate is essentially a litigation-liability vehicle funded by a CEO-owned DIP lender, attract U.S. Trustee scrutiny on disinterestedness and connections. The employment application at Dkt. 49 (filed August 10) is too recent to have drawn a deadline-compliant response by August 12 under standard notice periods. Until the full text of Dkts. 51, 52, 53, 56, and 57 is reviewed on PACER, their precise targets remain unverified; the desk flags this and will confirm at next update. What is clear from the docket structure — two oppositions plus a supporting declaration filed the same day as a separate objection — is that at least two distinct contested matters were briefed simultaneously on August 12, a pattern inconsistent with ordinary course and consistent with coordinated creditor or U.S. Trustee opposition.

The Errors/Deficiencies notice at Dkt. 59 (BNC, August 13) and the Generic Order at Dkt. 60 (August 13) are almost certainly related: the deficiency notice identifies a filing that failed to meet local-rule requirements, and the generic order likely resolves or memorializes the correction. This is procedural and carries no independent weight on recovery, though a deficiency on a retention or compensation filing could slow the authorization clock. Dkts. 54 and 55 are certificates of service, and Dkt. 58 is a proof of service (CSD 3010); all three are filing infrastructure and are omitted. The stipulation at Dkt. 57 is substantive in classification — stipulations in contested Chapter 11 matters affect legal rights — but its substance is unverified; if it reflects an agreed resolution of one of the contested matters briefed the same day, it is material to recovery posture, and the desk will confirm.

The contested posture on these professional-retention and compensation matters matters for creditors beyond the immediate cost. 
The two principal judgments — approximately $245 million in the De la Torre class action and approximately $157 million in the CFPB tribal-lending action — together with roughly $45 million in additional pending litigation and about $5 million in trade debt and professional fees, constitute substantially all of the debtor's prepetition obligations
, against reported assets of $1 million to $10 million. In that context, professional fees and CRO compensation drawn from the estate — funded by a ~$4 million DIP facility 
owned by the debtor's CEO
 — are not administrative minutiae; they directly compress whatever is available to unsecured creditors. Vigorous opposition to these applications signals that at least one party is treating the fee burn as a recovery issue, not a routine creditor courtesy. The next concrete milestone is the August 19 opposition deadline on the CRO compensation notice (Dkt. 43), which will either close the briefing on that motion or extend it if further responses arrive — and, depending on the scope of Dkt. 56's objection, the court may consolidate argument on the professional matters at a single hearing.

items.body_md:
On August 11, the SEC and CFTC filed parallel civil complaints against Goliath Ventures Inc. and CEO Christopher Delgado in the U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Florida — *SEC v. Goliath Ventures Inc. et al.*, No. 6:26-cv-01741, and *CFTC v. Goliath Ventures Inc. et al.*, No. 6:26-cv-01737. 
Both complaints allege that Goliath and Delgado orchestrated a crypto Ponzi scheme, raising roughly $400 million by soliciting funds purportedly for cryptocurrency liquidity pools and using investor money to pay earlier participants and fund personal spending; the SEC's complaint puts investor intake at at least $425 million from more than 1,300 investors through an unregistered securities offering.
 
The CFTC's complaint, drawing on a different investor universe, alleges approximately 1,600 customers contributed at least $397 million to the fraud.
 The two figures are not necessarily inconsistent — the agencies' jurisdictional theories overlap rather than co-terminate, and the pool of claimants in the Chapter 11 likely spans both populations.


The CFTC complaint alleges the scheme ran from at least November 2022 through February 2026, with Goliath misappropriating all customer funds while issuing account statements reflecting profits the company had not earned; Delgado, who the CFTC says was never registered with the agency, is named as a controlling person liable for Goliath's conduct.
 
According to the complaint, the money moved three ways: at least approximately $87 million paid fictitious returns to existing customers, at least approximately $174 million flowed to Goliath directors and staff as recruiting commissions, and Delgado personally extracted at least approximately $48 million for luxury homes, vehicles, and jewelry.
 
The SEC separately alleges Delgado misappropriated $51 million for homes, cars, and a yacht.
 
Delgado has agreed to a bifurcated settlement with the SEC
 — meaning liability is conceded but monetary relief remains to be determined by the court — while 
the CFTC is seeking restitution, disgorgement, civil monetary penalties, trading and registration bans, and a permanent injunction against further violations of the Commodity Exchange Act.


For the bankruptcy estate, the civil actions are a double-edged development. On the recovery side, they put two federal regulators formally in the queue as potential claimants or co-enforcement actors, which could complicate the receiver's ability to negotiate a clean plan and will need to be weighed against the September 30 proof-of-claim bar date in Case No. 26-13174-RAM. 
The Defiant notes the CFTC complaint expressly acknowledges the ongoing Southern District of Florida bankruptcy as the forum where customer recoveries are currently running,
 which signals the agency does not intend to pursue a competing distribution outside the estate — a meaningful concession for creditor recovery posture. On the risk side, the forfeiture obligations Delgado admitted at the time of his guilty plea, and any restitution or disgorgement ordered in these civil actions, will compete with unsecured creditors for the same depleted asset pool. 
The allegations in both civil complaints remain unproven, and counsel for Delgado and Goliath Ventures was not identified in the CFTC's announcement.


The next hard deadline is September 30, 2026 — the proof-of-claim bar date in Case No. 26-13174-RAM. Creditors who have not yet filed, and any claimants newly on notice from the SEC and CFTC press releases, must file by that date or risk being barred. Delgado's criminal sentencing before the Middle District follows on October 8, 2026, at which point the court will set restitution and forfeiture amounts that directly bear on what assets remain available to the estate.
